opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should start with a confession, which is that I'm not exactly a neutral party here. My brother Blake spent years writing an enormous biography of Warhol, so Andy has been something like an extra member of the family at our dinner tables for a long time. I've absorbed a great deal of Warhol by osmosis, whether I wanted to or not.

But I do think he's tremendously important, and I'd put it this way. One of the things I study is how children learn. Children are constantly figuring out what the categories of the world are, what counts as what. A lot of the most interesting art of the twentieth century does something similar for adults. It takes the categories we thought were settled, like what counts as art, what counts as a valuable object, what counts as worth looking at, and it shakes them loose so you have to figure them out again.

Warhol did that more radically than almost anyone. You put a Brillo box or a soup can in a gallery and suddenly you're forced to ask, what's the difference between this and the thing in the supermarket? Arthur Danto made that the centerpiece of his whole philosophy of art. The question isn't really answered by looking harder at the object, because the objects can be perceptually identical. It's answered by the whole context, the theory, the institutions, the conversation around it. That's a genuinely deep philosophical insight, and Warhol got there with a kind of deadpan that made it look effortless.

The other thing I find interesting, as a psychologist, is that he had this almost childlike quality of attention. He looked at the things everybody else had stopped seeing, the logos, the celebrity photos, the stuff of everyday commercial life, with the kind of fascination a two-year-old has for a shiny wrapper. Adults learn to filter all that out as boring. Warhol refused to filter it out. And in doing that he showed us something true about the world we actually live in, rather than the world we pretend we live in.

So: important, yes, maybe the most important American artist of the second half of the century. Whether every individual piece is great is a separate question, but the shift he produced in how we see is enormous.

r001.rationale: The response says Warhol radically unsettled ideas about what counts as art and describes the shift he produced in how people see.

r002.rationale: It grounds Warhol’s importance in changing how people understand art and what is worth looking at, presenting that shift as a measure of his achievement.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'm not an art historian, so take this with a grain of salt. But I think Warhol is actually enormously interesting from the perspective of someone who studies how minds work, and particularly how children's minds work. What Warhol did was take the completely ordinary, the soup can, the Brillo box, the celebrity photograph, and he made you look at it again. And that's very close to what I think of as the fundamental intellectual project of the child, or for that matter the scientist. Young children look at things that adults have stopped seeing because they've become so familiar, and they see them as strange and new and worth attending to.

So there's this way in which Warhol is doing something that's almost the opposite of what we usually think art does. The Romantic idea is that the artist has some special inner vision that they're expressing. Warhol's idea was more like, no, the vision is already out there in the world, in the supermarket and the tabloids, and the artist's job is just to shift your attention so that you notice it. That's an attentional move more than an expressive one, and I find that genuinely profound.

Now, is he a great artist in the sense of someone whose individual works I'd want to spend hours in front of? I'm less sure. I think the importance is more in the idea than in any particular silkscreen. But ideas that change how everybody afterwards sees things, that's not a small accomplishment. And he was also very funny, which I think people underrate.

r001.rationale: The response describes Warhol’s practice as shifting attention to ordinary images and contrasts it with the idea of art as expressing an artist’s inner vision, crediting him with changing how art is understood.

r002.rationale: It says ideas that change how people see things are a significant accomplishment, presenting that influence as a basis for judging Warhol’s artistic importance.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the things that makes Warhol interesting is that he gets you to look again at things you’ve stopped seeing. A soup can or a publicity photograph is so familiar that you barely notice it. Then he puts it in this different context, and suddenly you’re asking, “What am I actually looking at? Why does this image have the power that it does?”

There’s something quite profound about that, even if you don’t find the work beautiful. Art can change what we pay attention to, and Warhol is a striking example of someone who did that.

r001.rationale: The response says Warhol makes viewers look differently at familiar images, but does not say he reshaped how people think about artistic practice.

r002.rationale: It presents changing attention as something art can do, but does not identify changing how people think about art as a criterion of artistic achievement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think he’s important, but I find him more interesting as someone who changed the questions we ask about art than as someone whose work I love looking at. There’s something fascinating about taking an utterly familiar object—a soup can, a publicity photograph—and making you attend to it differently. Repetition can make something seem banal, but it can also make it strange.

The question for me is how much of that comes from the work itself and how much comes from knowing the idea behind it. With Warhol, I’m often more engaged by the idea. That’s a real artistic achievement, but it’s a different kind of achievement from making something that keeps rewarding you when you look at it.

r001.rationale: The response says Warhol changed the questions people ask about art and describes how his work makes viewers attend to familiar objects differently.

r002.rationale: It explicitly calls engaging viewers through the idea behind the work “a real artistic achievement,” linking artistic achievement to changing how people think about art.
